name: p3-0305-nested-try-routing
title: Where an exception lands: the stack of active try statements
spec: A call chain action1 to action2 to action3 drawn as stacked frames, with try markers. action1 has 'try: action2() except TypeError: print(Outer try)'. action2 has 'try: action3() except TypeError: print(Inner try); raise'. action3 runs 'print(1 + [])' which raises TypeError. Arrow from action3 up to the most recently entered try in action2: 'Python returns to the most recent matching try; only this first match handles it; Inner try is printed'. Then the bare raise (orange) sends it to action1: 'Outer try runs only because action2 re-raised'. Output box '$ python3 nested_exc_normal.py: Inner try, Outer try'. Variant lane 'try with only finally': 'each finally runs as the error moves up the stack; it does not stop the error; Inner try, Outer try, then the traceback: TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: int and list'. Loop variant 'for func in (raise1, noraise, raise2): try / except IndexError / finally / print(...)': table 'raise1: caught IndexError, finally run, ...', 'noraise: finally run, ...', 'raise2: finally run, then Traceback SyntaxError'. Rules strip 'once an except block finishes, execution continues after the try statement, not at the line that raised; Python does not undo earlier changes: L.append(added) stays in L and a global assigned before the error stays changed; local variables in exited functions are lost'. Bottom bar: 'Handler routing is a matter of runtime control flow, not only of how the statements are written'.
alt: Three nested functions where a TypeError is caught by the most recent try, re-raised with a bare raise and caught again, with the finally-only and loop variants and what survives an exception.
cap: The most recently entered matching try handles the exception first, and an outer handler runs only if the inner one re-raises.

name: p3-0305-exception-group
title: ExceptionGroup and except*: each handler takes its matches and the rest move on
spec: A flow. Top box 'action3 raises ExceptionGroup(Nest*, [IndexError(1), TypeError(2), SyntaxError(3)])'. Arrow to 'action2: except* IndexError: print(Got IE)' which takes IndexError and lets the other two pass. Arrow to 'action1: except* TypeError: print(Got TE)' which takes TypeError. Remaining 'SyntaxError(3)' reaches the top level (orange) and prints '+ Exception Group Traceback ... ExceptionGroup: Nest* (1 sub-exception) ... SyntaxError: 3'. Output box 'Got IE, Got TE, then the traceback'. Side panel 'Why': 'a script that waits on a whole rack of hosts can fail in several ways at once, and one exception object cannot carry them all; Python 3.11 added ExceptionGroup', 'in except* IndexError as E: each E is bound to a sub-ExceptionGroup of the matches, available as E.exceptions', 'unmatched exceptions continue upward in a new ExceptionGroup', 'one try statement can run multiple except* clauses', 'asyncio.TaskGroup uses this mechanism (chapter 3.6)'. Limits strip 'you cannot mix except* with a plain except in the same try; you cannot put return, break or continue inside an except* clause'. Contrast 'plain except: the first matching handler consumes the whole exception'. Bottom bar: 'A group keeps moving until every item in it has been matched'.
alt: An ExceptionGroup of IndexError, TypeError and SyntaxError passing through two except* handlers that each consume their match, leaving the SyntaxError for the top-level traceback.
cap: Each except* clause takes the exceptions it matches and passes the rest upward until the group is fully handled.

name: p3-0305-chain-and-unbind
title: Chaining errors with from, and why the as variable disappears
spec: Two panels. Panel 'Exception chaining': three forms. 'raise ConfigError(...) from exc: sets __cause__, makes the translation from a low-level error to a domain error explicit' (example load_config: FileNotFoundError becomes ConfigError(config file not found: path) from exc). 'raise NewError(...) with no from: Python still chains implicitly and shows During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred'. 'raise ... from None: use when the original error is only noise'. 'bare raise: re-raises the current exception with its traceback'. Handles list 'exc.args, str(exc), repr(exc), exc.__traceback__, exc.add_note(hint) (3.11), traceback.format_exc(), logging.exception() inside a handler'. Panel 'except Exc as var scope' (orange): code 'X = 99; try: 1 / 0; except Exception as X: print(X); saveit = X' then 'after the block: X is unbound (NameError: name X is not defined); saveit is ZeroDivisionError(division by zero)'. Reason line 'the traceback's frames hold local variables; if var stayed bound the exception would point back at itself through the frame, a reference cycle that delays garbage collection; Python runs del var when the block exits, even if var held a value before the try'. Fix 'assign the exception to a separate variable inside the handler if you need it later'. Bottom bar: 'Chain to translate errors, and copy the exception if you need it after the block'.
alt: Exception chaining with from, implicit chaining and from None, plus the rule that the except as variable is unbound after the block so the exception must be copied to another name.
cap: raise from sets __cause__ to make an error translation explicit, and the as variable is deleted when the except block ends.

name: p3-0305-ctxmgr-enter-exit
title: How a context manager handles errors: __exit__ returning True, and the generator form
spec: A timeline for 'with LookingGlass() as what:'. Step 1 '__enter__(self) patches sys.stdout.write so printed strings come out reversed, and returns JABBERWOCKY to the as what variable'. Step 2 'the body runs'. Step 3 '__exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback) restores sys.stdout.write'. Branch 'if exc_type is ZeroDivisionError it logs a divide-by-zero message and returns True, which suppresses the exception; any other return value lets the exception continue' (orange). Right panel 'Generator form': '@contextlib.contextmanager def looking_glass(): try: yield JABBERWOCKY except ZeroDivisionError: ... finally: sys.stdout.write = original_write'; reason 'an unhandled exception in the with body is thrown into the generator at the yield point through gen.throw(exc), so the restore step belongs in the finally block where nothing can skip it'. Panel 'ExitStack': 'for a dynamic number of managers: with ExitStack() as stack: files = [stack.enter_context(open(f)) for f in filenames]; unwinds registered callbacks and managers in LIFO order on exit'. Syntax strip 'several managers: with expr1 as v1, expr2 as v2:; Python 3.10 and later allows parentheses across lines: with (open(lines1.txt) as input, open(uppers.txt, w) as output):'. Comparison strip 'try/finally is the general tool; with works only with objects that support it; open file: myfile = open(...); try: ... finally: myfile.close() versus with open(...) as myfile'; 'CPython closes files when garbage-collected, but timing is unpredictable and a leaking process runs out of descriptors'. Bottom bar: 'Returning True is the switch that suppresses an exception'.
alt: The enter, body and exit steps of a LookingGlass context manager where __exit__ returns True to suppress ZeroDivisionError, with the contextmanager generator form and ExitStack.
cap: __exit__ always runs, returning True suppresses the exception, and the generator form needs try and finally around the yield.

name: p3-0305-exceptions-as-signals
title: Exceptions as control flow: leave nested loops, signal end of input, signal a result
spec: Three panels. Panel 'Leave several loops': 'class Exitloop(Exception): pass; try: while True: while True: for i in range(10): if i > 3: raise Exitloop; print(loop3: i) ... except Exitloop: print(continuing)'; output 'loop3: 0, loop3: 1, loop3: 2, loop3: 3, continuing, i=4'; note 'break exits only one level, with break here you get an infinite loop; i keeps its value because assignments in a try are not undone; the raise works like a goto where the except clause is the label, and you can jump only out of code wrapped in a try'. Panel 'End of input is a signal': 'while True: try: line = input() except EOFError: break else: process the line'; 'file read methods return an empty string at end of file, input raises EOFError; an empty string from input is a blank line, not the end'; 'other signal exceptions: sys.exit() raises SystemExit, Ctrl+C raises KeyboardInterrupt'. Panel 'Signal a result' (orange): 'class Found(Exception); searcher raises Found() on success; caller: try searcher() except Found: success else: failure' versus 'class Failure(Exception); searcher returns founditem or raises Failure(); caller: try: item = searcher() except Failure: not found else: use item'; reason 'if every object can be a valid return value, no sentinel such as None is safe; an exception carries the failure without touching the return value'. Bottom bar: 'In Python every error is an exception, but not every exception is an error'.
alt: Three exception idioms: raising Exitloop to leave three nested loops, EOFError ending an input loop and Found or Failure exceptions replacing sentinel return values.
cap: A raise can leave several loops at once, EOFError marks the end of input, and exceptions can return results that no sentinel value could.

name: p3-0305-too-broad-narrow
title: Catching too much and too little: three real failure stories
spec: A three row story table plus a design fix. Row 1 'sys.exit(62) inside bye(); caller has an empty except': 'SystemExit is a subclass of BaseException; the bare except catches it; the program prints Got it and then Continuing... instead of terminating'. Row 2 'x = myditctionary[key] in a try with except: x = None': 'the misspelled name raises NameError, the handler swallows it and fills in None, a typo becomes silent data corruption and the traceback that would have pointed at the line is gone; catching Exception here would do the same; list KeyError instead' (orange). Row 3 'func() has an inner bare except while the caller waits for IndexError': 'everything comes to the inner handler and dies; the outer try never sees it'. Opposite failure 'except (MyExcept1, MyExcept2): breaks if you add MyExcept3 later'. Fix panel 'class categories: class NumErr(Exception) with Divzero(NumErr), Oflow(NumErr), Uflow(NumErr); except mathlib.NumErr: also catches future subclasses such as Uflow without editing the except list; General category with Specific1 and Specific2'. Exception object panel 'FormatError(Exception) stores line and file attributes and a logerror method; positional arguments land in exc.args and str(exc); override __str__, not __repr__; derive from Exception, never a standalone class; name by condition, such as NodeUnreachable; a Combust subclass can override __str__ to print Call the fire department!...'. Tools strip 'atexit runs code at shutdown; sys.excepthook changes what the top-level handler does; os._exit ends immediately and skips cleanup, including atexit handlers and finally'. Rules of thumb strip 'wrap operations that often fail (file opens, socket calls); cleanup that must run belongs in try/finally or with; servers, test runners and GUIs must catch and recover, a one-shot script often skips handling'. Bottom bar: 'Be neither too general nor too specific, and choose the size of each try wisely'.
alt: Three failure stories of a bare except swallowing sys.exit, a misspelled dictionary name turning into silent None and an inner catch-all hiding IndexError, with category classes as the fix.
cap: A bare except catches SystemExit and NameError typos, while catching a category superclass handles future subclasses without edits.

name: p3-0305-assert-warn-excinfo
title: assert, warnings and the three ways to see the current exception
spec: Three panels. Panel 'assert': 'assert cond, message works like if __debug__: if not cond: raise AssertionError(message)'; 'python -O sets __debug__ to False and compiles every assert out'; (orange) 'never use assertions for input validation or security checks: the check disappears in exactly the builds that matter'; 'assert 1 < 0, Not in this universe! raises AssertionError with that message'. Panel 'warnings': 'warnings.warn(x is deprecated, DeprecationWarning, stacklevel=2): stacklevel 2 blames the code that made the call; control with -W flags and filters; tests can turn them into errors'. Panel 'Current exception, three ways' with the example 'class E(Exception): pass; try: raise E(info) except E as X': 'print((type(X), X)); print(sys.exc_info()[:2]); print((type(sys.exception()), sys.exception()))' all printing '(class __main__.E, E(info))'. Facts 'sys.exc_info() returns (type, value, traceback), or three None values if no exception is being handled; sys.exception() (3.11) returns the instance, the same as sys.exc_info()[1]; the traceback is usually in the instance's __traceback__; documentation calls exc_info old-style, but both work'. Traceback panel 'traceback.print_exc(file=open(badly.txt, w)) writes the error text to a file while Bye prints to the screen; read tracebacks bottom up: the last line names the error and the lines above show who called whom; do not depend on the exact text'. Outer try for debugging 'wrap the program in an outer try, empty except, print sys.exc_info()[0] and [1]; a test driver logs FAILED name or PASSED name and keeps going'. Bottom bar: 'Use the instance's own methods instead of checking its type'.
alt: Three panels on assert and python -O, warnings with stacklevel, and the three equal ways to read the current exception, with traceback.print_exc writing to a file.
cap: assert disappears under python -O, stacklevel 2 blames the caller, and sys.exception returns the same instance as sys.exc_info()[1].

name: p3-0305-eight-rules
title: Eight rules for error handling in tools and services
spec: A numbered table of the eight rules with a one-line example each. '1 Fail fast on programmer errors and invalid input: validate config and arguments at the boundary, right away, with clear messages'. '2 Handle expected operational failures where you can do something sensible: network timeouts, missing files, 404s, lock contention; retry with backoff, skip with a log, fall back, or translate into a domain error'. '3 Do not catch what you cannot handle: let unexpected exceptions bubble up to one top-level handler that logs the traceback and exits non-zero'. '4 Preserve information: chain exceptions, include host, path or request id, log tracebacks once rather than at every level'. '5 Make cleanup unconditional and idempotent: with or finally'. '6 Be explicit about partial failure: processing 500 hosts, collect results per host, report a summary, exit non-zero if any failed; do not abort at the first error, do not hide failures' (orange). '7 Limit retries to transient errors and idempotent operations: exponential backoff with jitter and a cap, limit attempts and total time, log each attempt; tenacity, backoff or a small helper from chapter 3.1'. '8 Set timeouts everywhere, on network and subprocess calls, because the default is often forever'. Right panel 'Conventional exit codes': '0 success', '1 general error', '2 usage or argument error, also used by argparse', '126 or 127 command not executable or not found', '128+N killed by signal N: 130 is SIGINT, 143 is SIGTERM', 'EX_TEMPFAIL 75 requests a retry', 'use documented codes when CI, systemd or schedulers must tell them apart'. Bottom bar: 'The exit code is the only part of a failure that the caller always sees'.
anchor: ### Error-handling strategy for tools and services
alt: A table of eight error-handling rules from failing fast to timeouts everywhere, beside the conventional exit codes 0, 1, 2, 126, 127, 128 plus N, 130, 143 and 75.
cap: Validate early, handle only what you can recover from, report partial failure honestly, and use conventional exit codes.

name: p3-0305-logging-setup
title: Logging rules: who configures, which level, which destination
spec: A two column layout. Left 'Rules': 'print for program output, logging for diagnostics with levels, destinations and structure'; 'levels DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL, set through configuration or environment variables, not by editing code; setup_logging(verbosity): 0 gives WARNING, 1 gives INFO, anything higher DEBUG'; 'use %s placeholders, not f-strings: arguments are formatted only when the record is emitted' (orange); 'one logger per module: log = logging.getLogger(__name__)'; 'libraries get a logger and add logging.NullHandler(); applications configure handlers once at startup'; 'log.error(..., exc_info=True) attaches the current traceback; log.exception() inside except does the same at ERROR level'; 'do not log inside tight loops at INFO: log summaries and sampled details, include units'. Right 'Destinations': 'stderr is a good default, stdout stays clean for data; containers and systemd capture it into the journal', 'RotatingFileHandler, TimedRotatingFileHandler, SysLogHandler, SocketHandler, QueueHandler for non-blocking logging', 'logging.config.dictConfig for declarative setups', 'in containers log to stdout and stderr and let the platform ship them'. Bottom panel 'Structured logging': 'JSON lines with fields such as host, job_id and duration_ms; structlog, python-json-logger or a custom Formatter; include a correlation or request id; redact secrets and personal data'. Format example '%(asctime)s %(levelname)-8s %(name)s: %(message)s'. Opening story 'the useful line scrolled away and the next run overwrote the file'. Bottom bar: 'Applications configure handlers once, libraries never do'.
alt: Logging rules for levels, lazy percent-s formatting, one logger per module, NullHandler for libraries and destinations from stderr to rotating files and structured JSON lines.
cap: Applications configure handlers once at startup, libraries only add NullHandler, and log calls use percent-s so formatting happens only when emitted.

name: p3-0305-flush-fsync
title: Where written bytes really are: Python buffer, OS cache, disk
spec: A left to right path of four boxes. 'f.write(text) into the Python buffer (a staging area in memory so many small writes become a few large ones)' then 'f.flush() pushes it to the OS' then 'os.fsync(f.fileno()) forces the data onto disk (durability, for example before you rename a checkpoint)' (orange) then 'on disk'. Mode table 'open(path, r, encoding=utf-8, errors=strict, newline=None)': 'r read text', 'w truncate and write', 'a append', 'x exclusive create, fails if it exists', '+ read and write', 'b binary'. Notes 'text mode decodes and encodes with the encoding you pass and translates newlines; always specify the encoding; binary mode returns bytes and does no decoding', 'buffering=0 makes a binary file unbuffered; line buffering from buffering=1 or the -u flag', 'always use with: it closes the file even when an exception occurs; never leave file handles to the garbage collector'. Large files strip 'for line in f streams line by line; read() loads the whole file, only for small files; chunked reads iter(lambda: f.read(1<<20), b""); mmap.mmap(f.fileno(), 0, access=mmap.ACCESS_READ) for random access without copying; os.sendfile and shutil.copyfileobj'. Bad bytes strip 'errors=replace, backslashreplace or surrogateescape; only surrogateescape round-trips arbitrary bytes'. Story 'a log file is empty because the process died before its buffer reached the disk'. Bottom bar: 'Do not declare success before an fsync'.
alt: The path of written data from the Python buffer through flush to the OS and fsync to disk, with the open modes, buffering options and large file reading techniques.
cap: flush moves data to the OS, fsync moves it to disk, and with closes the file even when an exception occurs.

name: p3-0305-secure-create
title: Creating files safely: exclusive open, 0600 from the start, and unique temp names
spec: Three rows contrasting unsafe and safe. Row 'secret file': unsafe 'create the file, then chmod it afterward: readable to others while it waits' ; safe (orange) 'os.open(path, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL, 0o600): restrictive mode from the start; check your 0o octal literals'. Row 'create only if missing': unsafe 'if not exists: create, which leaves a gap another process can enter (TOCTOU, time of check to time of use)'; safe 'attempt the operation and handle the exception: open(..., x), os.mkdir, Path.mkdir(exist_ok=True)'. Row 'temp files': unsafe 'build temp names yourself in /tmp: predictable names enable symlink attacks and collisions'; safe 'tempfile.mkstemp() makes unique files with mode 0600; TemporaryDirectory(), NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False), mkdtemp(); clean up with context managers; place large scratch data by setting TMPDIR'. Side panel 'Permissions calls': 'os.chmod, os.chown, os.umask, Path.chmod, stat modes such as stat.S_IRUSR; os.access exists but beware TOCTOU races'. Side panel 'Overlapping runs': 'fcntl.flock(fd, LOCK_EX | LOCK_NB) is advisory (enforced only for programs that ask) and released when the process exits; other options: os.open with O_CREAT | O_EXCL, the filelock library, the flock command, database or etcd leases for distributed locks; sample: BlockingIOError then sys.exit(another instance is running)'. Archive strip 'tarfile with untrusted archives: a member name such as ../ writes outside the chosen directory; use filter=data on 3.12 or later, or validate each member; rmtree is dangerous, validate the path first; shutil.copy2 preserves metadata; hashlib.sha256 streams a digest in 1 MiB chunks'. Bottom bar: 'Attempt the operation and handle the failure instead of checking first'.
alt: Unsafe and safe ways to create secret files, check-then-create races and temp files, with advisory flock for overlapping runs and the tarfile path traversal warning.
cap: Create secrets with O_EXCL and 0600 in one step, let mkstemp pick temp names, and attempt then handle instead of check then create.

name: p3-0305-encoding-settings
title: Four encoding settings, and the 5, 7 and 5 byte worked example
spec: Left panel 'AÄBèC': 'len = 5 characters'; '.encode(utf-8) = 7 bytes: b"A\xc3\x84B\xc3\xa8C" (the two accented characters need 2 bytes each)'; '.encode(latin-1) = 5 bytes: b"A\xc4B\xe8C" (one byte per code point from 0 to 255)'; '.encode(ascii) raises UnicodeEncodeError (no room for either accent)' (orange). Code point examples 'ord(a) == 97 == 0x61, ord(Ä) == 196 == 0xc4, ord of the smiling face == 128578 == 0x1f642'. Centre panel 'Four settings that cause surprises': 'sys.getdefaultencoding() returns utf-8', 'locale.getpreferredencoding(False) is the default for open() when you omit encoding=; with LANG=C it can be ANSI_X3.4-1968 or ASCII; on Windows cp1252', 'sys.stdout.encoding controls print output, PYTHONIOENCODING overrides it', 'sys.getfilesystemencoding() covers OS file names; os.listdir and os.walk return str for a str directory and bytes for a bytes directory such as os.walk(b".")'; fix 'set PYTHONUTF8=1 or -X utf8 (PEP 540, 597, 686), and still pass encoding="utf-8" explicitly'. Right panel 'Error and BOM cases': 'UnicodeDecodeError: bytes not valid in the assumed encoding; UnicodeEncodeError: the target codec cannot represent some characters; errors=ignore, replace, xmlcharrefreplace, backslashreplace', 'diagnose with file -i, chardet, charset-normalizer or bytes.decode(utf-8, errors=replace)', 'opaque filenames: os.fsdecode and os.fsencode with surrogateescape (PEP 383) maps each lone byte 0x80..0xFF to U+DC80..U+DCFF and restores the exact bytes', 'BOM: utf-16-le starts b"\xff\xfe", utf-16-be starts b"\xfe\xff", utf-8-sig strips the UTF-8 BOM b"\xef\xbb\xbf"'. Bottom bar: 'Always pass encoding="utf-8": a setting you wrote down is one you can read again in six months'.
anchor: ## 4. Text, bytes and encodings in practice
alt: The string AÄBèC at 5 characters, 7 UTF-8 bytes and 5 Latin-1 bytes, the four Python encoding settings, error handlers, surrogateescape and BOM prefixes.
cap: The same five characters take 7 bytes in UTF-8 and 5 in Latin-1, and locale defaults differ between hosts, so always pass the encoding.

name: p3-0305-unicode-compare
title: Comparing text correctly: NFC, casefold, accents and byte patterns
spec: A table of five traps with the fix. 'caf\u00e9 (len 4) versus cafe\u0301 (len 5, e plus a combining acute accent): both render as café but s1 == s2 is False' / 'unicodedata.normalize(NFC, s) on both, then nfc_equal(s1, s2) is True; W3C recommends NFC; NFKC and NFKD also convert compatibility characters: the one-half sign becomes 1 fraction-slash 2, the micro sign becomes Greek mu; the Ohm sign U+2126 normalizes to Greek capital Omega U+03A9 under NFC'. 'Case-insensitive comparison' / 'normalize with NFC then .casefold(): Straße.casefold() == strasse; fold_equal in Fluent Python does this'. 'Strip accents without damaging Greek or Cyrillic' / 'shave_marks_latin: decompose with NFD, drop each unicodedata.combining(c) mark only when the base character before it is in string.ascii_letters, recompose with NFC: São Paulo: Zéphyr & Ελληνικά becomes Sao Paulo: Zephyr & Ελληνικά'. 'Sort accented words in human order such as caju, atemoia, cajá, açaí, acerola' / 'locale.strxfrm or pyuca.Collator()'. 'Regular expressions on text versus bytes' / 'str pattern r\d+ matches ASCII and Unicode digits, including Tamil digits; bytes pattern rb\d+ matches only ASCII 0 to 9; pass re.ASCII to a str regex for that behaviour'. Footer strip 'struct for binary protocols: struct.pack(">i4sh", 7, b"code", 8) gives b"\x00\x00\x00\x07code\x00\x08"; struct.unpack(">i4sh", B) returns (7, b"code", 8); network order is big-endian, written ! or >; also struct.pack("<IHB", 1, 2, 3), unpack_from, int.from_bytes(b, big), .to_bytes(4, little), memoryview, bytearray'. Protocol encodings strip 'HTTP headers Latin-1 or ASCII; JSON must be UTF-8; YAML UTF-8 or UTF-16; spreadsheet CSV may use utf-8-sig or cp1252; open CSV with newline=""'. Bottom bar: 'Normalize before you compare'.
anchor: ## 4. Text, bytes and encodings in practice
alt: A table of Unicode comparison traps, composed versus decomposed café, casefold, shaving accents with NFD and NFC, locale sorting and str versus bytes digit patterns, plus struct.pack layout.
cap: Two strings that look identical can differ in code points until you normalize them, and a bytes regex matches only ASCII digits.

name: p3-0305-format-traps
title: Data format cheat sheet: purpose, safe call and trap
spec: A table with columns 'Format', 'Use for', 'Safe call', 'Trap'. 'JSON' / 'machine interchange' / 'json.loads, json.dumps(data, indent=2, sort_keys=True, ensure_ascii=False, default=str)' / 'float precision, large integers, NaN, duplicate keys; JSON Lines for streaming: for line in open(events.jsonl): json.loads(line)'. 'YAML' / 'configs people edit by hand' / 'yaml.safe_load, yaml.safe_dump(sort_keys=False), yaml.safe_load_all for multi-document manifests; ruamel.yaml preserves comments' / 'never yaml.load on untrusted input (arbitrary object construction); the Norway problem: region: no becomes boolean False' (orange). 'TOML' / 'tool settings' / 'tomllib.loads (read-only stdlib since 3.11; tomli-w to write)' / 'no stdlib writer'. 'CSV' / 'tabular exports' / 'csv.DictReader and DictWriter with newline="" and encoding' / 'spreadsheets may use utf-8-sig or cp1252; large data: pandas (chapter 3.10)'. 'INI' / 'legacy config' / 'configparser: cp[db].getint(port, fallback=5432)' / '-'. 'Parquet or JSON Lines' / 'large datasets' / '-' / '-'. Rules strip 'validate parsed data with a schema or pydantic; handle JSONDecodeError and YAMLError with file and line context; never eval data'. Time panel 'datetime.now(timezone.utc) for aware datetimes; time.monotonic() for durations, immune to clock changes; time.time() wall clock; time.perf_counter() for benchmarks; zoneinfo.ZoneInfo(Europe/Berlin) for time zones; datetime.fromisoformat and ISO 8601 with a timezone; store UTC and log in UTC; avoid naive datetimes'. Story strip 'a metrics export contains NaN that the next tool in the chain refuses to read'. Bottom bar: 'Choose each format for its purpose, and parse with the safe call'.
alt: A table of JSON, YAML, TOML, CSV and INI with their purpose, safe call and trap, including the Norway problem and yaml.load, plus which time function to use.
cap: Use safe_load for YAML, newline empty for CSV, and aware UTC datetimes with monotonic clocks for durations.

name: p3-0305-injection-and-run
title: Shell injection in two examples, and the run() helper that prevents it
spec: Left comparison with two attack stories. 'A file called gpu report.csv pasted into a command string becomes two arguments' and 'a hostname from a spreadsheet arrives with a semicolon, so the script runs two commands instead of one'. Unsafe 'shell=True with interpolated text: metacharacters ; $() backticks && quotes and globs turn a name into command injection'. Safe (orange) 'subprocess.run([kubectl, get, nodes, -o, json], capture_output=True, text=True, encoding=utf-8, errors=replace, check=True, timeout=30, env={**os.environ, KUBECONFIG: ...}, cwd=/tmp)'. Right flow of the run() helper: 'log.info(exec: shlex.join(cmd))' then 'dry_run? return CmdResult(tuple(cmd), 0, "", "")' then 'subprocess.run(... timeout=timeout)' with branches 'TimeoutExpired becomes OpsError(timeout after Ns: cmd) from exc', 'FileNotFoundError becomes OpsError(command not found: cmd[0]) from exc', 'check and returncode != 0 becomes OpsError(cmd exited rc: first 500 chars of stderr)', else 'CmdResult(cmd, rc, out, err) frozen dataclass'. Facts strip 'CalledProcessError has returncode, stdout, stderr and cmd; a negative returncode means killed by that signal, -9 is SIGKILL; capture_output buffers all output in memory, stream when huge; input=data sends stdin; stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL stops prompts hanging; text was called universal_newlines; if a shell is needed quote each dynamic part with shlex.quote or build pipelines with Popen'. Prefer-library strip 'socket and ipaddress, psutil, os.statvfs and shutil.disk_usage, platform, pwd and grp, pyudev, netifaces or pyroute2, docker and kubernetes clients, boto3, paramiko, pynvml or nvidia-ml-py instead of nvidia-smi; machine-readable output: -o json, ip -j, lsblk -J, nvidia-smi --query-gpu=... --format=csv,noheader,nounits'. Security strip 'never run executable names that users control; shutil.which(kubectl); in privileged scripts pin absolute paths and scrub PATH; sudo -n for non-interactive; do not pass secrets on the command line because ps shows them: use environment variables, stdin or 0600 files'. Bottom bar: 'Give every subprocess a timeout and an argument list, and check its return code'.
alt: Two shell injection stories beside safe subprocess.run arguments and the flow of a run() helper that logs, supports dry run, applies a timeout and turns failures into OpsError.
cap: An argument list stops a space or semicolon from becoming a second command, and a run() helper adds logging, dry run, timeout and clear errors.

name: p3-0305-process-tree
title: Streaming a child, building a pipeline, and killing the whole tree
spec: Three stacked lanes. Lane 'Stream with a deadline': 'Popen([ping, -c, 5, 10.0.0.1], stdout=PIPE, stderr=STDOUT, text=True, bufsize=1)'; 'deadline = time.monotonic() + 30; for line in p.stdout: handle(line); if past the deadline: p.kill(); break'; 'rc = p.wait()'. Lane 'Pipeline without a shell: dmesg | grep -i error | tail -20': p1 'Popen([dmesg], stdout=PIPE)' to p2 'Popen([grep, -i, error], stdin=p1.stdout, stdout=PIPE)' to 'p1.stdout.close() so p1 can receive SIGPIPE if p2 exits' (orange) to p3 'run([tail, -20], stdin=p2.stdout, capture_output=True, text=True)'. Lane 'Kill the whole tree on timeout': 'p = Popen(cmd, start_new_session=True)' then 'os.killpg(os.getpgid(p.pid), signal.SIGTERM)'. Side facts 'deadlock avoidance: communicate(), capture_output=True, merge stderr=STDOUT, threads, or asyncio.create_subprocess_exec (chapter 3.6)', 'a zombie is a finished child whose exit status nobody collected; wait() and communicate() reap children; unreaped children linger as <defunct>' with the character symbols written without angle brackets as 'defunct', 'services and daemons: use Popen and manage the lifecycle yourself'. Bottom bar: 'Reap every child, and kill the process group, not just the parent'.
alt: Three lanes for streaming a child with a monotonic deadline, building a dmesg grep tail pipeline without a shell and killing a whole process group, with zombie and deadlock notes.
cap: Stream with a deadline, close the first pipe end so SIGPIPE works, and use a new session so killpg can end the whole tree.

name: p3-0305-cron-vs-shell
title: Why a script works by hand and fails at 2 a.m.: what the environment changes
spec: A two column comparison 'Run by hand' and 'Under cron or systemd', with rows. 'Python: the one in your venv' / 'a different Python'. 'PATH: your full PATH' / 'a shorter PATH'. 'Current directory: where you are' / '/'. 'Terminal: a TTY to print to' / 'no terminal'. Further differences from the interview note 'env, locale, umask, user, HOME, signals'. Right panel 'What the script can read about its world': 'os.environ.get, os.getenv(X, default), os.environ.copy(); sys.argv, sys.executable, sys.platform; platform.node(), machine(), release(); os.getpid(), getppid(), getuid(), geteuid()'; 'len(os.sched_getaffinity(0)) gives usable CPUs and respects cgroups and affinity better than os.cpu_count()' (orange); 'resource.getrlimit and setrlimit(RLIMIT_NOFILE, (65536, 65536))'; 'os.nice, os.sched_setaffinity, os.setsid'. Panel '/proc, /sys and psutil': 'psutil.cpu_percent(interval=1, percpu=True), virtual_memory(), disk_usage(/), net_io_counters(pernic=True), process_iter([...]), Process(pid).children(recursive=True)'; 'open(/proc/meminfo), Path(/sys/class/net/eth0/speed), Path(/proc/loadavg)'; 'values come back as text; files can vanish when a process exits, so handle FileNotFoundError and ProcessLookupError'; 'containers see namespaced and cgroup-limited views such as /sys/fs/cgroup/...; psutil totals may show the host rather than your limit, so a script can believe it has far more memory than it may use'. Rules strip 'use argparse, do not parse sys.argv by hand; configuration and secrets in environment variables injected by systemd or Kubernetes; never log them wholesale'. Bottom bar: 'The script did not change, the world around it did'.
alt: A comparison of running a script by hand versus under cron or systemd, with the calls that read the process environment, usable CPUs, /proc, /sys and psutil and the container limit trap.
cap: Under cron or systemd the Python, PATH, working directory and terminal differ, and inside containers psutil can report host totals instead of your limit.

name: p3-0305-sigterm-pid1
title: A Kubernetes stop: SIGTERM, the grace period, SIGKILL, and Python as PID 1
spec: A timeline. 't0 Kubernetes sends SIGTERM' to 'handler runs in the main thread between bytecode instructions: log.warning(received SIGTERM, shutting down); stop.set()' to 'main loop: while not stop.is_set(): do_work(); stop.wait(5) (interruptible sleep)' to 'finish the in-flight item, checkpoint, cleanup()' then 'terminationGracePeriodSeconds elapses' then 'SIGKILL (cannot be handled)' (orange). Handler registrations strip 'SIGTERM: Kubernetes or systemd stop', 'SIGINT: Ctrl-C', 'SIGHUP: reload_config() by convention', 'SIGPIPE set to SIG_DFL: script | head ends quietly'. Rules panel 'keep handlers tiny: set a flag and do the real work in the main loop, because a handler that opens a file or waits on the network can be interrupted in the middle of its own work; SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be handled'. PID 1 panel 'inside a container Python running as PID 1 does not reap zombies or forward signals by default: use tini, docker run --init, or exec the process from a shell wrapper; in the lab compare with and without --init under docker stop and its grace period'. Exit hooks strip 'atexit.register(fn) runs on normal exit, but not on SIGKILL or os._exit; faulthandler.enable() dumps tracebacks on crashes; faulthandler.register with kill -SIGUSR1 dumps them on demand'. Bottom bar: 'Use the grace period to finish in-flight work and checkpoint'.
alt: A timeline of SIGTERM setting a stop flag, the loop finishing its item and cleanup, the grace period ending in SIGKILL, and the PID 1 zombie and signal forwarding caveat with tini.
cap: Set a flag in the handler, finish the in-flight item inside the grace period, and use an init process so PID 1 reaps zombies and forwards signals.

name: p3-0305-drain-template
title: The drain_nodes template: flow and the qualities to copy
spec: A flow for 'drain_nodes --selector pool=gpu-a --max-failures 0 --dry-run -v'. Step 1 'parse_args' then 'logging to stderr, level by -v count (WARNING, INFO, DEBUG)'. Step 2 'signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM set a stop Event'. Step 3 'select_nodes: kubectl get nodes -l selector -o json'; branches 'OpsError: log.error, return 2' and 'no nodes: log.warning, return 0'. Step 4 loop 'for each node: drain(): if stop.is_set(): Result(node, False, interrupted); kubectl cordon (idempotent); kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --timeout=300s; Result(node, True) or Result(node, False, str(exc))'; 'stop when failures exceed --max-failures (failure budget)'. Step 5 'print JSON to stdout: drained list and failed list' (orange) then 'return 1 if failed else 0'. Side note 'dry-run: kubectl returns an empty string for drain, cordon, uncordon and delete'. Qualities checklist 'a single main() returns the exit code', '--dry-run previews the work', 'each step idempotent so a second run does no harm', 'each node isolated from the others with a failure budget', 'every subprocess has a timeout', 'logs go to stderr and machine-readable results go to stdout', 'handles interrupts gracefully', 'no shell', 'error messages include the command and its stderr', 'small testable functions; sequential for safety (rolling), parallelise cautiously'. Bottom bar: 'When one of the qualities is missing, ask whether the omission was deliberate'.
anchor: ## 8. A template for robust operational scripts
alt: The flow of the drain_nodes script from argument parsing and signal handlers to node selection, a cordon and drain loop with a failure budget and JSON output, with the checklist of qualities.
cap: The template returns exit codes from main, previews with dry run, isolates each node with a failure budget and keeps logs on stderr and results on stdout.

name: p3-0305-mistakes
title: Common mistakes in errors, files and subprocesses, grouped
spec: A four group table 'Area' and 'Mistake' and 'Fix'. Group 'Exceptions': 'bare except and except Exception: pass; catching too much around too much code loses tracebacks and hides bugs' / 'catch the narrowest exception, log once at the top'. Group 'Files': 'writing in place leads to partial writes; declaring success before an fsync; exists-then-create checks leave gaps; no explicit encoding; mixing bytes and str' / 'atomic replace, fsync, attempt then handle, encoding=utf-8'. Group 'Subprocess': 'shell=True with interpolated input; missing timeouts; ignored return codes; parsing human-formatted output; secrets in command lines; capturing huge output in memory; pipe deadlocks; unreaped children; os.system, os.popen and the deprecated commands module' / 'argument list, timeout, check, machine-readable output, communicate, wait'. Group 'Global state': 'mutating os.environ or os.chdir inside a library affects every caller; assuming the current directory' (orange) / 'copy the environment for the child, pass explicit paths'. Group 'Re-runs': 'scripts unsafe to re-run' / 'dry-run mode, a lock against overlapping runs, UTC timestamps rather than naive ones'. Group 'Signals': 'heavy work in signal handlers; ignoring SIGTERM in containers' / 'set a flag, finish and exit'. Group 'Untrusted input': 'extracting tar or zip archives without validating paths; yaml.load or pickle on data from the network' / 'validate member paths, filter=data, safe_load'. Stories strip 'a cleanup script runs twice because its lock was checked before it was taken, and the second run deletes the checkpoint the first one was writing'. Bottom bar: 'A second attempt after a failure should be boring'.
alt: A grouped table of mistakes in exceptions, files, subprocesses, global state, re-runs, signals and untrusted input, each with its fix.
cap: Most mistakes are too-broad handlers, unsafe file and process handling, shared global state and scripts that are not safe to re-run.
